extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and students of dramatic theory (writers of tragedy)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing tragedy: selecting and handling tragic incidents, constructing plot (complication and denouement), creating characters, staging recognitions, diction and sensory effects, and using the chorus. Emphasises necessity/probability, unity, and modes of artistic recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and handling of shocking familial incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should look for situations such as a brother killing a brother, a son his father, a mother her son, a son his mother, or other deeds of that kind; he may not destroy the received legends but ought to show invention of his own and skilfully handle the traditional material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred modes of presentation are limited: (1) the action done consciously with knowledge (e.g. Euripides' Medea); (2) the deed done in ignorance with the tie of kinship discovered afterwards (e.g. Sophocles' Oedipus); (3) to be about to act with knowledge and then not to act (ranked as worst—'shocking without being tragic'); (4) to be about to do an irreparable deed through ignorance and discover before it is done (best—e.g. Merope spared her son in Cresphontes, Iphigenia recognizing her brother). The poet should prefer the more artful kinds of presentation (natural recognition, prevented deed) and avoid the least effective (knowing then not acting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve traditional framework but show invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should not destroy the framework of the received legends (the fact that Clytemnestra was slain by Orestes, Eriphyle by Alcmaeon, etc.), but ought to show invention of his own and skilfully handle the traditional material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not abolish canonical facts of the mythic material; instead rework episodes, recognitions and scenes with originality. Skillful handling means making incidents serve the tragic effect while respecting the source material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: goodness (moral purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: First and most important: character must be good. Any speech or action that manifests moral purpose of any kind will be expressive of character: the character will be good if the purpose is good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goodness is relative to each class (even a woman or a slave may be 'good' within their social type). Use moral purpose in actions and speeches to convey character. Examples of failure: motiveless degradation (Menelaus in the Orestes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: propriety (appropriateness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Second aim: propriety. A character must be appropriate to their type—valour that is 'manly' is not appropriate to a woman; certain cleverness may be inappropriate to some types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose traits fitting to social/sexual/type class. Inappropriate traits make character unconvincing (e.g. an 'manly' courage presented as a general characteristic of women is inappropriate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: likeness to life (probability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Third aim: character must be true to life; a person of a given character should speak or act in a given way, by rule either of necessity or of probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters and incidents should proceed by necessary or probable sequence. Avoid actions or speeches that violate what would be expected from the character or situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: consistency (even consistent inconsistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fourth aim: the 'smooth' or consistent—though the model from life may be inconsistent, the dramatist must keep that inconsistency consistent (i.e., a character may be inconsistent but must be consistently inconsistent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid motiveless or arbitrary changes in character (example of inconsistency: Iphigenia at Aulis whose later self does not resemble earlier portrayal); ensure continuity and believable development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions and unravelling must arise from the plot (necessity/probability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The complication and the unravelling must arise out of the plot itself; do not bring about the unravelling by external artifices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid Deus ex Machina for events internal to the drama (e.g. not as in Medea or the return of the Greeks in the Iliad); Deus ex Machina may only be used for antecedent or subsequent events outside the drama's human range. Ensure causal or probable links within the plot so that both complication and unravelling seem natural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude irrational elements from the action
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the action there must be nothing irrational; if irrationality cannot be excluded, it should be outside the scope of the tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irrational occurrences that cannot be justified by the plot should be placed outside the action proper or treated as events attributed to gods (example: the irrational element in Sophocles' Oedipus is treated as external).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation: ennoble the original (the painter analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy imitates persons above the common level; the poet, like a good portrait-painter, should reproduce the distinctive form of the original but make the likeness truer to life and more beautiful (ennoble defects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve the type while enhancing its nobility—e.g., portray Achilles as noble even when irascible or indolent. Keep the essential features but idealise artfully where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sensory appeals (but not as essentials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals to the senses are concomitants of poetry: they are not among the essentials but there is much room for error in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ sensory detail to augment effect, but avoid allowing sensory ornamentation to contradict or distract from the plot, character, or probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anagnorisis (Recognition): prefer recognitions arising from the incidents themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition (anagnorisis) has several kinds: by signs (tokens, congenital or acquired marks), by a turn of incident, invented recognitions (poetically spoken revelations), by memory (an object or sight awakens remembrance), and by process of reasoning; composite kinds (false inference) also exist. Of all recognitions the best is that which arises from the incidents themselves where the startling discovery is made by natural means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rankings and examples: recognitions by signs/tokens and formal proofs are least artistic; recognitions invented at will by poet (e.g. a character gratuitously declaring identity) are near faults; recognition by incident (e.g. Odyssey bath scene) and recognition by memory/ reasoning are superior; the best are those emerging naturally from the action itself (e.g. Oedipus, Iphigenia). Avoid clumsy token-based or author-imposed revelations; aim for recognitions that feel inevitable from the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds and treatment of tokens/signs in recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Tokens/signs used for proof may be congenital (e.g. a spear, stars) or acquired (scars, necklaces, the ark). Such tokens admit of more or less skilful treatment; using tokens 'for the express purpose of proof' is a less artistic mode of recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using tokens, strive for naturalness (e.g. Odysseus' scar recognized by nurse in one way and by swineherds in another). Avoid contrived token-revelations that feel like mere proof devices rather than organic parts of the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid recognitions invented at will by the poet
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions invented at will—where a character simply speaks or reveals what the plot does not require—are nearly allied to the fault of artificiality and are considered weak art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on characters unexpectedly declaring identity or facts because the poet wants a discovery; let revelations be demanded by the plot's logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition by memory and by process of reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition by memory: sight or hearing awakens memory (e.g. seeing a picture, hearing a song) leading to tears and recognition. Recognition by reasoning: characters infer identity by logical steps (e.g. 'someone like me has come; no one resembles me but X; therefore X has come').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These modes are more artistic than tokens; use sensory triggers and plausible reasoning to effect believability. Beware of false inference or composite recognitions that depend on incorrect expectations (e.g. the disguised Odysseus/bow example) which can produce artificiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot construction through vivid visualization and staging
rubrics_metrics.description: In constructing the plot and wording, the poet should place the scene as far as possible before his eyes—seeing everything with vividness like a spectator—so as to discover what is in keeping and avoid inconsistencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work out appropriate gestures and staging; ensure on-stage facts are visible and understandable (example: Carcinus' oversight where Amphiaraus's route was not made clear offended the audience). Use visualization to spot logical or presentational errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sketch general outline first, then fill episodes; episodes must be relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the story is taken ready-made or constructed, the poet should first sketch its general outline, then fill in and amplify episodes. The episodes must be relevant to the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the main skeleton (e.g. Iphigenia outline) and only include episodes that contribute to the whole. Keep episodes short in drama and ensure they serve the plot (e.g. madness and purificatory rite in Orestes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity vs. epic multiplicity: avoid epic structure in tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy must not adopt an epic structure with multiplicity of plots (an 'epic system' or 'poly-mython'); in epic the length permits many parts, but in drama such multiplicity leads to failure or poor performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select portions of larger tales rather than dramatizing whole epics (criticises dramatising the entire Iliad or entire Niobe story). Maintain unity and appropriate magnitude for the drama's parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic structure: Complication and Unravelling (Dénouement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy falls into two parts—Complication (from the beginning to the turning-point of good or bad fortune) and Unravelling (from the beginning of the change to the end).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose the complication to lead convincingly to the turning-point, and have the unravelling follow naturally from that cause. Use this two-part analytic framework when designing plot progression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genres/kinds of tragedy and combination of elements
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four kinds of tragedy: the Complex (dependent on Reversal and Recognition), the Pathetic (motives = passion), the Ethical (motives = ethical), and the Simple (exhibits the marvelous/spectacular). The poet should endeavour to combine as many poetic elements as possible, or at least the most important ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to integrate reversal, recognition, ethical motive, and pathos where appropriate; critics expect breadth of excellence. Be cautious about relying solely on spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Chorus as an integral actor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus should be regarded as one of the actors; it should be an integral part of the whole and share in the action (in the manner of Sophocles rather than Euripides).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the choral songs pertinent to the subject; avoid choral interludes that are mere entertainment or interchangeable between plays. The Chorus should contribute to the plot and emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (dianoia): speech effects—proof, refutation, and emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought includes every effect to be produced by speech: proof and refutation; the excitation of feelings such as pity, fear, anger; and the suggestion of importance or its opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic speeches should prepare and produce such effects. Treat incidents and speeches from the same points of view when aiming to evoke pity, fear, importance or probability—incidents should 'speak for themselves' without verbal exposition, while speeches must produce their effects through the speaker's words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction and Modes of Utterance (delivery belongs to different art)
rubrics_metrics.description: One branch of diction concerns the Modes of Utterance (command, prayer, statement, threat, question, answer, etc.), but the province of delivery/acting belongs to the art of Delivery rather than poetry alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of the kinds of utterance and their rhetorical uses; however, detailed delivery techniques are the actor's/artisan's domain. Ensure diction serves thought and the intended emotional effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of language elements and rhetorical figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Language comprises letter, syllable, connecting word, noun, verb, inflexion or case, sentence or phrase; forms and figures of speech (schemata of diction) belong to diction and rhetoric and affect poetic quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ appropriate rhetorical figures and grammatical forms to shape diction; balance what should appear without exposition and what must be supplied by speech. Familiarity with rhetorical method improves the poet's craft.
